domain: Software Engineering / Political Economy of Technology / Intellectual Property
topic_summary: Analysis of the free/open-source software versus proprietary software debate. The topic is framed by advocates as a foundational question of user freedom versus a pragmatic choice of development and business models. The debate centers on whether software source code should be publicly available with freedoms to use, study, modify, and share, or whether it should remain closed and licensed under proprietary terms.

key_entities: Free Software Foundation (advocacy organization promoting software freedom as ethical imperative)
Open Source Initiative (advocacy organization promoting open development as pragmatic methodology)
Proprietary software vendors (commercial entities distributing closed-source software under restrictive licenses)
End users (individuals and organizations consuming software)
Source code (the human-readable instructions that define software behavior)
key_tensions: User freedom vs vendor control (FSF framing vs proprietary model)
Collaborative development vs competitive advantage (open source methodology vs trade secret protection)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The moral and legal status of software source code access and modification rights
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Competing interpretive traditions: ethical/freedom-based (FSF), pragmatic/methodological (OSI), property-rights-based (proprietary), and hybrid utilitarian frameworks

readings.commitment: Software freedom is a fundamental ethical requirement; proprietary software is an injustice
readings.authority_grounding: Deontological ethics / natural rights tradition (FSF lineage)
readings.expected_structural_delta: All proprietary software enters victim set; users have inalienable rights to source access; licensing restrictions are categorically illegitimate constraints

readings.commitment: Open source is a superior development methodology; freedom is instrumental to quality
readings.expected_structural_delta: Proprietary software not inherently illegitimate; open development valued for peer review, bug detection, innovation velocity; permissive licensing acceptable

readings.commitment: Software is intellectual property; creators have legitimate right to restrict access and modification
readings.authority_grounding: Property rights tradition / labor theory of value / commercial law
readings.expected_structural_delta: Source code is proprietary asset; licensing restrictions are legitimate exercises of ownership; users are consumers with contractual rights only

readings.commitment: Software licensing should maximize aggregate welfare; both models serve different contexts
readings.authority_grounding: Consequentialist ethics / economic efficiency / pluralist frameworks
readings.expected_structural_delta: No categorical victim set; context-dependent optimization; infrastructure favors open, specialized tools may justify proprietary; mixed ecosystems acceptable

axiom_contradictions.basis: Freedom imperative holds that users have inalienable rights to source access that cannot be legitimately restricted; property rights reading holds that creators have legitimate authority to impose such restrictions. No single framework can hold both axioms simultaneously.

Freedom imperative treats proprietary software as categorically unjust regardless of consequences; utilitarian hybrid treats justice as context-dependent and outcome-based. A deontological framework cannot simultaneously hold that an action is categorically wrong and that its permissibility depends on aggregate welfare calculations.

axes.primary_observable: Vulnerability disclosure rates; time-to-patch metrics; exploit frequency by licensing model

omegas.description: Does AI training on open-source code constitute a new extraction mechanism not contemplated by original FOSS licenses? Copilot/LLM code generation may reclassify open source from commons to training corpus.

Do nation-states have legitimate authority to mandate source code access for security/sovereignty reasons, overriding both FOSS and proprietary frameworks? China's source code review requirements and EU digital sovereignty initiatives suggest a fifth reading.

The four readings are stable within current discourse, but the freedom_imperative vs pragmatic_development split (FSF vs OSI) may be a historical artifact rather than a structural necessity. A unified freedom-and-pragmatism reading may emerge.

Is commons_sustainability a true Snare (structural extraction) or a Piton (atrophied governance)? If FOSS communities could coordinate to impose contribution requirements, the constraint type changes.

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Four readings identified through multi-tradition lens scan (deontological, pragmatic, property-rights, consequentialist). Network effects and commons sustainability pass pairwise independence test as distinct structural mechanisms with different observables and beneficiary structures.
